title: Google Pixel at 10: Successes, failures, and fun along the way [Video]
snippet: A decade of Pixel, it’s only in the last few years that we have seen Google settle into a rhythm with smartphones. It hasn’t been smooth sailing, though. more…
fullText:
A decade of Pixel, it’s only in the last few years that we have seen Google settle into a rhythm with smartphones. It hasn’t been smooth sailing, though.

Look back at the line-up, and it’s still hard to believe we’ve had a decade of Pixel. If you asked me back in 2016 whether Google’s in-house hardware experiment would stick around long enough to reach fully custom 3nm silicon, I’m not sure I’d have believed you.

To say that Google was late to the market is an understatement. By 2016, Apple and Samsung were already well into the swing of things. To be fair, that still is the case a decade later, but now with an even tighter iron grip over the space. I was personally distraught when the Nexus lineup was canceled to the point that I actually went with the Galaxy S8 rather than wait to see what Google had in store next.

	

Google’s answer to the ‘big two’ was Pixel. A phone not “officially” made by partners, but still sort of relying on OEMs while the production pipeline or groundwork was laid.

Pixel and Pixel XL (2016)

The original Google Pixel was built in a close manufacturing partnership with HTC, featuring a wedge-shaped profile that famously tapered down to eliminate any camera bump. 

Let’s be real, the hardware wasn’t tearing up trees, and it looked more than a little similar to the iPhone 7/8 series. It was a conservative design, but pretty darn self-assured.

The main thing that helped differentiate the device was its built-in Google Assistant integration and HDR+ image processing pipeline for photos. Rightly or wrongly, this simple formula has more or less defined the Pixel for the past decade of Google’s mobile computing efforts.

Smart, simple software and artificial intelligence have been at the forefront from the very beginning and will remain so over the next 10 years.

Pixel 2 series (2017)

With the second generation, Google finally figured out design. The LG-made Pixel 2 XL gave us the iconic “Panda” colorway with its stark black-and-white glass back and the bright orange accent power button. You’ve told us time and time again that it’s a personal favorite for Pixel fans. It also debuted the Pixel Visual Core, Google’s first attempt at custom co-processing to let apps like Instagram use HDR+.

Add single-lens Portrait Mode that put dual-camera rivals to shame, squeeze-to-activate Active Edge, ambient Now Playing track identification, and the persistent At a Glance widget, and the Pixel 2 series genuinely felt like magic in your hand.

The first major problems started to appear, though. The blue shift on the 2 XL meant that viewing from an angle is not recommended. Screen burn-in was also something people suffered.

Pixel 3 series (2018)

The Pixel 3 era was peak camera software dominance mixed with a few just flat-out bizarre hardware choices. 

That Pixel 3 XL “bathtub” notch was an absolute eyesore and was thoroughly roasted by the tech community and reviewers alike. I think in some ways, once you fired up the camera, all was forgiven. I’ve taken some incredible photos with the Pixel 3. Pictures that I still look at very fondly 8 years later.

This was the first Pixel to come with Night Sight, which arrived via a software update and single-handedly changed low-light smartphone photography forever. It wasn’t the first, but it was one of the best implementations.

You could shoot in near pitch-black conditions and walk away with a clean, detailed photo without ever touching the flash. Pair that with yet more AI-powered functions such as Call Screen, which handles telemarketers and spam in real time, and the software was doing all the heavy lifting.

In trademark fashion, the Pixel 3 had issues with RAM management and poor battery life. It was a mixed bag, but it was followed up by something truly interesting because the Pixel 3a is one of the best midrangers ever. It set the stage for a change of pace…but that wasn’t for a couple of years.

Pixel 4 series (2019)

Let’s be honest, Google swung for the fences with the Pixel 4, but it didn’t quite land. 

It is almost the least Pixel-y of the entire lineup because it stands apart from all that have since followed. The black sheep in many ways. It ditched the trusty rear fingerprint scanner, they threw Project Soli into a chunky top bezel for wave-to-snooze Motion Sense gestures and 3D Face Unlock.

We also got a silky smooth 90Hz display and a telephoto lens rather than the industry-preferred and marginally more flexible ultrawide. It felt like a zig to everyone else’s zag.

Alas, it was a big risk and one that ended up compromising the most. The small Pixel 4 had a tiny 2,800 mAh battery that struggled to get through an afternoon, let alone a full day. High launch prices and Soli radar frequency restrictions in key markets meant commercial success was hard to come by, and the negatives really held back the lineup. It actually triggered a reshuffle in Google’s hardware team.

Pixel 4a, 4a 5G and Pixel 5 (2020)

Faced with global disruptions in 2020 due to the emergence of COVID-19 and maybe due to some, at the time, unknown future plans, Google completely pivoted with the Pixel lineup. The Pixel 4 was a big swing, but the follow-up series went in a very different direction.

The mid-range Pixel 4a launched at just $349/£349 and became an immediate hit because it kept that flagship-grade camera performance in an understated, no-nonsense plastic body. This was an appetizer for what was to come.

Then came the flagship Pixel 5, but this wasn’t the premium phone that many expected. It skipped top-tier Qualcomm silicon entirely for the upper-mid-range Snapdragon 765G. It was the same chip used by many cheaper phones and even the more affordable Pixel 4a 5G, which was basically a bigger, bolder version of the 4a.

The 5 was coated in a bio-resin finish over a recycled aluminum frame, it brought back the rear fingerprint scanner, swapped the telephoto for an ultrawide lens, and gave us uniform bezels with reliable battery life. It lacked raw processing grunt, but it earned a cult following for simply being a reliable, compact everyday phone.

On one hand, it was good to see Google right some issues with the previous generation. On the other hand, it was confusing as it sort of signaled that maybe Pixels were not high-end phones. It was a reset.

Pixel 6 series (2021)

After a fairly unassuming and, arguably, boring preamble, 2021 was without a doubt the biggest turning point in Pixel history. 

Google overhauled the design, introducing the now iconic camera bar running across the back, creating a silhouette you could spot from a mile away. We were given a proper two-tier lineup with a Pro phone that packed in a triple camera system, a larger 120Hz display, and a cheaper but still competent base model. 

Most importantly, though, was the debut of original Tensor (now G1) silicon. Moving away from standard Qualcomm chips meant Google could tailor hardware directly for on-device ML—powering features like Magic Eraser, Live Translate, and Material You dynamic color themes.

As well-received as it was at launch, the Pixel 6 had some serious growing pains with a slow optical fingerprint reader, terrible modem performance, and overheating issues galore, but despite what were fairly major issues, the foundation was set.

Pixel 7 series (2022)

The Pixel 7 and 7 Pro took the foundational groundwork of the Pixel 6 and smoothed out the rough edges. Visually, the camera bar evolved into a seamless piece of 100% recycled aluminum that flowed directly out of the side rails, swapping out the all-glass visor for a sleeker metal shell with pill-and-cutout camera cutouts.

Under the hood sat Tensor G2, which paired with an upgraded Samsung Exynos 5300 modem. This finally resolved the signal drops and battery drain that plagued the previous generation. While raw computational gains were modest, Tensor G2 unlocked key software capabilities: Photo Unblur in Google Photos (which could restore old, blurry archival photos taken on any camera), Macro Focus via the ultrawide lens, and the return of a fast 2D Face Unlock system.

Mid-2023 also saw the Pixel lineup expand its footprint. The Pixel 7a raised the bar for mid-range phones by bringing a 90Hz refresh rate and wireless charging to the A-series for the first time. Meanwhile, Google made its long-awaited entry into new form factors with the original Pixel Fold, showcasing a short, wide “passport” design that prioritized a usable outer display over tall, narrow screens. It was a bit of a “fail” in the sense that it didn’t move the needle and was quickly overshadowed by others due to launching with the previous-generation processor and, admittedly, strange aspect ratios.

Pixel 8 series (2023)

In my mind, the Pixel 8 and 8 Pro were the moment the lineup transitioned from an enthusiast recommendation with caveats to a phone you could comfortably recommend to everyday consumers. Never perfect, but quietly the last Pixel that felt truly like a Pixel. These are bubbly, friendly phones in all the ways that matter.

A few more AI functions made their debut: Best Take, Audio Magic Eraser, Video Boost, and, as a headline addition, 7 years of full updates for the first time. Basically, making these the industry standard for smartphone support. Google leapfrogged Samsung and even Apple for software support windows.

No, no reinvention of the wheel. Tensor still didn’t hit the heights many wanted, which is to say it was fine.

Pixel 9 series (2024)

The Pixel 9 was a rapid design departure in a number of ways. Firstly, it ditched the friendly, playful looks that had been a trademark of the series. Instead, it took a very boxy route that instantly felt familiar to anyone who may have tried an iPhone.

It was a really polished upgrade and sort of put to bed some of the tricky hardware issues that plagued many of the older Pixel models. Google also began leaning into yet more AI-powered functionality, with Gemini now being a key component.

Google unified the launch across all phones, coming on day one, but also switched from the standard October release cadence to a late-summer August release. Pitching the Pixel ahead of the iPhone has been a huge change. Allowing the company to lay out plans and getting even more hype around a launch lineup.

Pixel 10 series (2025)

Although on the surface, almost the exact same, the Pixel 10 was the first 3nm chip for the lineup, and it was the first to be fabricated by TSMC. It signaled the end of the Samsung Foundry partnership that was the start of the Tensor era.

Any lingering thermal issues were gone, Gemini was integrated even further and into even more places, like the camera, and the first steps of multimodel intelligence were added with Magic Cue. I’d stop short of saying the Pixel 10 delivers on some of the promises made way back on October 4, 2016, but it came as close as it ever had until that point.

Finally, we had a flagship-level device with Qi2 magnets at the back too. It took until 2025 for one of the biggest Android brands to adopt Magsafe or, in this case, Pixelsnap. With that one move, the Pixel 10 opened up a whole world of accessories to be attached without the need for a case. It’s so elementary, it’s a wonder we haven’t seen more try to do it.

Pixel 11 series (2026) and beyond

A decade later, we’re here with the Pixel 11. The peak of the Made by Google series thus far. There are still pain points, namely a design that hasn’t evolved too drastically, performance from the Tensor processor still feels decidedly mid-range at times, and a heavy emphasis on AI functionality to make up for this raw performance gap.

A sometimes lazy observation of the original Pixel was that it was the “iPhone of Android,” but that seems to have been taken to heart, and a decade after launch, we have the most “iPhone-y” Pixel to date. Maybe that is a symptom of where smartphones have stalled, but it’s a really interesting evolution. The advantage is that you know what to expect. Gemini is becoming more and more prominent and yet a more integral component in Pixel phones, and that isn’t likely to cease any time soon.

What’s easy to see is that Pixel has been a bigger success than the Nexus lineup. Getting hold of the full end-to-end user experience has helped drastically. I don’t think anyone can argue that the best Nexus phone is easily surpassed by the best Pixel phone.

It would be remiss of anyone talking about Google products without some fears over whether we’ll get another decade of Pixel, but with so many internal changes at the company and bigger marketing budgets thrown at actually marketing the devices, it seems that, at least for now, the Pixel is here to stay. 

The past decade has proved that Google was never really trying to build the highest-spec hardware on the market. Instead, Pixel has always been an engine designed to deliver Google’s software vision. From early HDR+ algorithms on single camera lens setups and now to custom TSMC Tensor silicon wired for Gemini integration, it’s hard to argue that Google’s Pixel has succeeded in changing how we evaluate a smartphone: not by how fast its CPU clocks, but by how helpful it is throughout the day.

Maybe sales will eventually catch up, but the main thing is to keep making solid devices, and playing the long game might start to be the best decision Google could have made after entering the market late.

There have been plenty of bumps in the road along the way, but here’s the next decade of Pixel. I’m sure it’ll be a wild ride.

title: These are the best times to save money on your next flight, according to Google Flights
snippet: Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, Google is detailing the best time to book your next flight to get the best possible price. more…
fullText:
Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, Google is detailing the best time to book your next flight to get the best possible price.

With surging fuel prices have also come much higher plane ticket costs and, with that, everyone’s looking for a deal. In a blog post this week, Google Flights details the best times to book your next flight.

For domestic US flights, the best time is apparently 39 days prior to departure, but the lowest price can fall anywhere between 57 days prior and 22 days prior to the actual flight date. International flights should be booked much further out, with 89 days being the magic number there.

Thanksgiving and Christmas flights bend the rules a bit. Thanksgiving flights are actually cheapest 34 days prior to departure, but Christmas flights need to be booked much earlier at around 56 days.

	

Here’s the full breakdown from Google:

Domestic flights: 39 days before departure (low price range is 22–57 days)

International flights: 89 days before departure, but the average price drop during the low range (50–133 days out) is insignificant

Thanksgiving: Lowest prices hit 34 days before departure (low price range is 21–57 days)

Christmas: 56 days before departure (low price range is 33–67 days)

Spring break: 50 days before departure (low price range is 29–64 days) for trips in March or April

Summer vacation: 21 days before departure (low price range is 20–47 days) for trips in July or August

Trips to Europe: 49 days or more before departure

Trips to Mexico or the Caribbean: 43 days before departure (low price range is 24–69 days)

The post goes on to detail trending destinations for the 2026 travel season, with Hawaii being the top Thanksgiving destination and international trips to Greece and Canada trending around Christmas and New Year’s Eve.

title: Google confirms Android Auto updates & fixes for media apps – the squiggly line is here to stay
snippet: New Android Auto updates tend to be a bit strange, with changes often showing up for some users but not others, but Google has just recapped a handful of Android Auto updates for media apps from the past few months, including confirmation that the squiggly line design is here to stay. more…
fullText:
New Android Auto updates tend to be a bit strange, with changes often showing up for some users but not others, but Google has just recapped a handful of Android Auto updates for media apps from the past few months, including confirmation that the squiggly line design is here to stay.

In a Reddit post by Google’s “Community Engagement Manager” for Android, five recent Android Auto updates are confirmed as either rolling out or widely available. The first is the ability to control media from any app, including YouTube and others. We noticed this rolling out back in March of this year for YouTube, and it has since rolled out to more apps. Today’s post confirms it is available for “browser audio streams, and niche media apps” and is designed to work with “any media app.” You can use it for play/pause and skip controls, but you can’t open an app to browse any other data.

Next up is the redesigned media app player that applies to apps like Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pocket Casts. The new design makes it easier to access playback controls and also better fits on a variety of different screen sizes.

This one has been showing up all year and started rolling out more broadly in July. Today’s post confirms that the in-app UI for media apps on Android Auto will start changing for some apps “in the next few months,” as announced in May.

	

Another new media-focused feature on Android Auto that’s been rolling out is the ability to swipe between active media sessions from the dashboard widget. If you start driving with one app and then switch to another, both will stay readily available for easy access.

A background improvement, Google’s post adds, has been made to autoplay. This includes making it so media apps that you haven’t recently used will “no longer be selected for autoplay,” while Android Auto will also now recognize if you frequently stop autoplay and offer a pop-up that lets you turn off the feature quickly. If you’ve ever noticed issues with autoplay starting even when you have it turned off right after your vehicle turns out, Google also says that a fix is being applied.

Finally, the post also confirms that the “squiggly line” media player design is here to stay. This one has been showing up for months, but has come and gone for many. Especially in the past few weeks, there have been dozens of reports of the redesign simply vanishing.

The updated design is apparently meant to “make it easier to see where you are in a track at a glance,” but Google is apparently listening for feedback on it – it’s been a rather divisive change among the Android Auto community.

title: Gemini app gains new ‘Map’ tool, replacing ‘/’ with ‘@’
snippet: Google has introduced a “Map” tool to aid your location-based Gemini app prompts on Android and iOS. Meanwhile, the Gemini app is already getting ready to replace the forward slash for skills. more…
fullText:
Google has introduced a “Map” tool to aid your location-based Gemini app prompts on Android and iOS. Meanwhile, the Gemini app is already getting ready to replace the forward slash for skills.

On mobile (not available on the web), you can find “Map” at the end of the carousel alongside Photos, Camera, Avatar, Files, Drive, and Notebooks. 

This launches a live map of your current location with a circular focus area. You can pan and zoom in/out as needed, while the magnifying glass icon in the top-right corner lets you search for any location. Once you’ve made a selection, hit “Explore this area.”

This adds “Map Area” to the prompt box where you can append text. The Map tool is widely rolled out.

	

With the latest Google app beta (version 17.63), Gemini is replacing the forward slash (“/”) to invoke skills with the “@” symbol that’s already used for Connected Apps, which will soon be renamed to “Connectors.”

Google just announced on Wednesday that skills will replace Gems and that you can use a slash in the prompt box to activate. We’re seeing the following prompt when entering a slash: 

/ is now @. Access your skills, connectors and more from a single place.

The box that appears is slightly wider than before, with skills appearing first and a shortcut to create new ones. This change is not widely rolled out yet.

More on Gemini app:

Google details Gems to skills migration, including free access

Gemini app adding Google Wallet integration for ‘personalized insights’

iOS 27.2 beta 3 details

Apple released iOS 27.2 beta 3 on Monday for developers, with build number 24B5099f. It comes two weeks after the release of the second beta. A new public beta was released on Tuesday, ahead of a final release to everyone before the end of the month.

What’s new in iOS 27.2 beta 3?

New Apple Music logo

Apple teased a new Apple Music logo when it announced Apple Music Hall last month, and iOS 27.2 beta 3 suggests it’s about to roll out everywhere. The new logo uses a bolder typeface than the old logo, plus a lowercase “m” in “music.”

New Messages settings in the works

Code references in iOS 27.2 beta 3 suggest Apple is working on a new setting that gives users more control over the suggested actions that appear in the Messages app, such as the “Add to Calendar” button.

The code hints that you’ll be able to disable suggested actions for individual apps, including Calendar, Reminders, Notes, and Maps. The change isn’t actually enabled yet, and it’s possible Apple scraps it before releasing it.

title: Google Antigravity Googlebook app hits the Play Store
snippet: Ahead of the Googlebook launch, Google Antigravity is now available in the Play Store. more…
fullText:
Ahead of the Googlebook launch, Google Antigravity is now available in the Play Store.

Antigravity is Google’s agent-first development platform, with version 2.0 released at I/O 2026 in May. It serves as a “dedicated mission control to work alongside, steer, and customize agents that operate autonomously in the background.”

After creating macOS, Windows, and Linux versions, Antigravity is now available on Android with a native interface. It interacts with the Linux environment available on the new laptops. You can “Create and deploy apps right on your Googlebook.”

The package name is com.google.android.apps.antigravity, and the app is currently on version 2026.09.23.988012583.

	

That said, it’s currently only available on Googlebook OS. The interface might work on tablets and foldables, but it’s unclear if Google designed it for smaller phone screens. 

The interface looks similar to the other desktop versions, but it remains to be seen whether it will retain feature parity given how quickly the other apps are updated with major features on a weekly basis.

Antigravity on Googlebooks is part of Google’s push to make the new platform suitable for developers. You can also just install the Linux version of Antigravity on Googlebooks, along with Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. Additionally, Google advertised the ability to install the Antigravity CLI via the Googlebook terminal.

fullText:
Apple’s major MacBook Pro overhaul is just around the corner, and should debut within a month or so. It’ll be the first touchscreen MacBook, as well as the first with Tandem OLED. Beyond that, though, the new MacBooks should be ‘significantly’ lighter than their predecessors, according to the latest issue of the Power On newsletter.

The newsletter reiterates that the new MacBook Pro should debut ‘by next month,’ so we should see these new machines before the end of November. These machines should offer the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, as Apple has opted to skip the higher-end part of the M6 family in favor of accelerating the M7 launch.

New MacBook Pro to be much lighter

Despite the fact that these MacBooks have been rumored for quite some time, we haven’t really known too much about them besides specs on paper: OLED, touch, Dynamic Island, and so on. In the past, reports have described the computer as thinner, but we haven’t really had much of a visual. We still don’t, but we do have one major new detail on what this machine will feel like:

The new MacBook Pros are lighter — significantly lighter. Apple has reengineered the machine’s interior miniaturizing parts and rearranging components to make the computer much easier to carry. The current 16-inch MacBook Pro weighs as much as 4.8 pounds, compared with 3.3 pounds for the 15-inch MacBook Air, so any meaningful reduction would be immediately noticeable.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman doesn’t specify exactly how much lighter it will be, but if you’re someone who uses a current-generation MacBook Pro, especially the 16-inch, you might find that it’s heavier than you’d like it to be. Apple is reportedly working to improve on that.

Beyond that, Gurman also mentions that there will be some changes in macOS Golden Gate to support touch and the Dynamic Island, alongside the debut of macOS 27.2.

title: HP’s MacBook Neo competitor is $699 with an OLED display and plenty of catches
snippet: The PC market was caught flat-footed by Apple’s MacBook Neo launch earlier this year, and while that laptop’s aggressive pricing strategy has already been forced to adapt to market conditions, it’s only months later we’re seeing Windows-based rivals announce their own respective competitors. Today, it’s HP’s turn, with a brand-new OLED-equipped laptop set to start at that same $699 price point, but not without plenty of strings attached. more…
fullText:
The PC market was caught flat-footed by Apple’s MacBook Neo launch earlier this year, and while that laptop’s aggressive pricing strategy has already been forced to adapt to market conditions, it’s only months later we’re seeing Windows-based rivals announce their own respective competitors. Today, it’s HP’s turn, with a brand-new OLED-equipped laptop set to start at that same $699 price point, but not without plenty of strings attached.

	

The HP OmniBook 5 14 effectively looks like a cross between the MacBook Neo’s low-cost, colorful chassis and the more refined, understated greens and blues found in Apple’s iPad Air lineup. At 11.77mm thick and just 2.56 pounds for a 14-inch display, it sounds perfect for the back-to-school shopping season HP just barely missed. That 14-inch display is the real star of the show, though, swapping the usual IPS panels in this price point for one of two OLED options — more on that in a moment. Along the frame, HP’s packed in two “full-function” USB-C ports and a headphone jack, while a FHD camera with Windows Hello support greets you anytime you open the screen.

Under the hood, HP says it’ll support “up to” an Intel Core 7 processor, though that’s the only option on display here. Battery performance sounds impressive on paper — up to 42 hours of local video playback via an unspecified capacity — but I’ll admit that local video playback tests aren’t exactly ideal for mirroring onto actual real-world use. HP does say it’s compatible with the company’s 65W mini GaN charger, which I assume is bundled in the box. Otherwise, dual mics and “Poly Studio-tuned” audio wraps up what we know about this device so far, and if you’re feeling like there’s plenty you still don’t know, you aren’t alone.

For starters, it’s unclear what processor the $700 variant of this laptop will ship with, leaving comparisons with Apple’s A18 Pro hard to make. HP also chose to omit storage and memory configuration information of any kind — not even an “up to” — which really demonstrates just how beaten down the PC market is in the midst of this ongoing RAM crunch. Even the highlight of this laptop comes with a pretty nasty catch; while HP spends the bulk of the post describing its 2.5K OLED panel, that version won’t ship until March of 2027. The variant hitting Best Buy later this month will include a 2K OLED panel, with a massive dip in brightness from 650 nits all the way to just 300.

	

Lots of unanswered questions — and some disappointing answers — but if HP still has your attention, look for more details ahead of its retail release.

title: Apple may soon track when Google promotes Chrome inside Safari
snippet: Apple may be preparing to track when Google promotes Chrome or the Google app to users browsing in Safari, and how users react to those promotions. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple may be preparing to track when Google promotes Chrome or the Google app to users browsing in Safari, and how users react to those promotions. Here are the details.

Since iOS 27.2 beta 2, Apple has been testing code in Safari that can detect when Google shows banners promoting Chrome or the Google app on its search pages, as well as whether users interact with those promotions.

While this does not mean that Apple will ship this telemetry feature when iOS 27.2 officially launches, it does suggest that Apple is at least experimenting with a way to measure how often Google promotes its own apps to Safari users and how those users respond.

It is currently unclear why Apple is testing the feature. However, the new code comes amid heightened regulatory scrutiny of competition between Safari and rival browsers, including how users are steered toward alternatives such as Chrome.

In the UK, for instance, Google has specifically cited its efforts to promote Chrome to iPhone users as evidence that it continues to compete with Safari, while regulators have examined whether the companies’ search agreement reduces their incentives to compete in browsers.

In the European Union, in turn, Apple is also subject to Digital Markets Act requirements around browser choice and defaults, with the European Commission previously investigating whether its Safari choice screen complied with those rules.

	

So whether Apple intends to collect and use this data for its own benefit or as part of an effort to address growing regulatory scrutiny over browser competition remains to be seen.

What the code does establish is that Apple has built Safari to detect and log those interactions, and the system works like this: Safari injects a .js script into certain Google home and search results pages, which looks for visible promotional banners or other Google page elements intended to encourage users to open or install Chrome or the Google app.

Safari then looks for links associated with either app, including their custom URL schemes and App Store IDs. If it detects a promotion, it can log certain events, including whether the banner was shown, whether the user appears to be signed in to a Google account, and whether the user interacted with the promotion. This allows Apple to categorize the interaction as either accepted or dismissed and log that result.

As of iOS 27.2 beta 3 and Safari 27.2 beta release notes, Apple has yet to publicly document the feature.

title: Acclaimed British comedy series ‘Small Prophets’ now available on Apple TV
snippet: The first two episodes of “Small Prophets” are now available to stream on Apple TV, following a wave of glowing reviews for the British comedy series. Watch the trailer below. more…
fullText:
The first two episodes of “Small Prophets” are now available to stream on Apple TV, following a wave of glowing reviews for the British comedy series. Watch the trailer below.

’Small Prophets’ now streaming on Apple TV

Earlier today, my colleague Ryan covered the raving reviews for “Small Prophets,” a British comedy series Apple TV acquired for international distribution earlier this year.

The move marked a first for Apple TV, as the streamer had never previously acquired an existing English-language series that had already aired elsewhere.

“Small Prophets” premiered on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two in the U.K. earlier this year, before Apple picked it up for international distribution in August.

It is now available to Apple TV subscribers globally, except in the U.K., where it will arrive on the service in 2027.

“Small Prophets” was created, written, and directed by Mackenzie Crook (Detectorists), who also stars alongside Pearce Quigley (The Way Back), Lauren Patel (The Effects of Lying), Sir Michael Palin (Monty Python), Sophie Willan (Ludwig), Jon Pointing (Big Boys), and Paul Kaye (Game of Thrones), among others.

Following the two-episode premiere, the show will run every Wednesday through November 4.

Here’s Apple TV’s synopsis of “Small Prophets”:

“Small Prophets” is a comic tale of the eccentric Michael Sleep (Pearce Quigley) who, since his darling Clea disappeared seven years ago, has lived a very ordinary life. He works in a DIY store, visits his dad Brian (Sir Michael Palin) and hopes for Clea to return. One day Brian shares an old recipe involving rainwater, horse manure and more than a little alchemy. With recipe in hand, Michael sets out (albeit with some skepticism) to create homunculi — magical spirits that can predict the future — in the hope they have the answer to his burning question: “will I ever see Clea again?”

Michael gets help from his young coworker Kacey (Lauren Patel), an unlikely friendship that blossoms partly (but not wholly) through their mutual dislike of store manager Gordon (Mackenzie Crook). Their friendship adds to the frustration and intrigue of his nosy neighbors (Sophie Willan, Jon Pointing) who are obsessed with trying to find out what the hell is going on in the garden shed.

fullText:
I’m in the middle of testing Dell’s 32-inch UltraSharp U3226Q, and my thoughts so far are extremely positive. The picture quality of this OLED panel is impressive, especially when HDR is enabled in macOS. I’ll have a full hands-on review of the UltraSharp on our YouTube channel.

Meanwhile, I wanted to note a key improvement Apple introduced in macOS 27 regarding HDR support. A drawback of using an HDR-ready third-party monitor on macOS 26 Tahoe was the inability to activate High Dynamic Range at the common 2560 x 1440 scaled resolution. Fortunately, the newest macOS release resolves this problem.

The problem

If you’re using an HDR10-capable third-party display with macOS Tahoe, you’ll see a High Dynamic Range toggle in Settings → Displays. When that switch is flipped, HDR content will be viewable. You can see an example of this in the screenshot below.

macOS Tahoe with High Dynamic Range enabled at 1920×1080

But notice in that same screenshot that I’m running the display at a resolution of 1920 x 1080, which is exactly 2x the pixel-doubled resolution of this 4K UHD display’s native 3840 x 2160.

Most users probably don’t want to run at 1920 x 1080 because it makes content appear too large on a 4K display. The Dell Ultrasharp U3226Q is a 32-inch display, and running at 1920×1080 greatly reduces the available screen real estate.

Fixing this issue in macOS is easy; simply select a scaled resolution, such as the popular 2560 x 1440, which is the default setting for Apple’s 5K Studio Display. The problem is that when you select a scaled resolution on macOS Tahoe, HDR is disabled. Notice the screenshot below:

The HDR option is disabled when using 2560×1440 scaled resolution on macOS Tahoe

As you can see, the High Dynamic Range toggle is no longer available, and macOS automatically switches back to Standard Dynamic Range. This means that when running macOS Tahoe with an HDR display, you have to choose between HDR and running the preferred scaled resolution.

Thankfully, this issue has been fixed in macOS 27 Golden Gate. In the screenshot below, you can see that you can have both a scaled resolution selected and HDR enabled simultaneously. This is a native option, and no third-party software is involved.

macOS Golden Gate fixes the ability to run HDR with a 2560×1440 scaled resolution

So if you’re running a third-party HDR display, this feature alone makes upgrading from macOS Tahoe to macOS Golden Gate worth it, in my opinion. Granted, this is on my M4 MacBook Pro. I tried the same thing on my M1 Max MacBook Pro, but I couldn’t select both settings at the same time, even though I was running macOS 27, so there are apparently hardware requirements as well.

macOS Golden Gate includes a range of new features, which I outlined in my Siri AI overview, my macOS Top Features video, and my final review of macOS 27. One such feature related to HDR displays is that macOS 27 offers much more native HDR support across the OS.

EDR/HDR support in macOS Golden Gate

You’ll notice super-bright spectral highlights, cursors, and an overall more contrasty appearance compared to macOS Tahoe. It all results in a fantastic look for both Apple Studio Display XDR users, Pro Display XDR users, and third-party OLED display users.

What are your thoughts? Do you run a third-party external display with your Mac, and if so, would you consider using an HDR-capable display?

fullText:
Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Most people know that Amazon collects data about your shopping history to serve up personalized product recommendations. But what some of us didn’t realize is that you can check exactly what Amazon knows — or thinks it knows — about you in your settings menu. One user’s findings went viral on Threads after she discovered that Amazon assumed she “has flat buttocks” based on her purchases, resulting in a flood of other posts with users sharing the oddly specific information Amazon uses to describe them.

In another post, a user found that Amazon says they don’t “trust people easily,” while someone else discovered that Amazon thinks she “finds it hilarious when toys get stuck to ceiling tiles in the classroom.” Other descriptions spotted by users include “cusses when scared,” “cannot keep real plants alive,” “has no friends,” and “treats cats as biological children.”

While some of these descriptions seem like a roast from Amazon, most of them are pretty generic. For example, mine says I “maintain active aquarium systems,” “regularly consume coffee,” and “play video games regularly,” all of which are accurate.

If you want to see what Amazon may have learned about you, you can find out by selecting your account icon in the top-right corner of your screen, scrolling down to the “Your Account” section, and hitting “Your Shopping preferences.” From there, scroll down the page and select “About You.” You’ll then see a list of details Amazon uses to personalize your account, which you can edit or delete.

Good morning! Today, I’m searching for Prime Day deals, watching Chris Rock masterfully dodge questions about The Slap, questioning Sam Altman about whether we have to accept “some bad things” to justify AI’s exponential growth, and brushing up on my chess game after many years of neglect.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

When Google bought Fitbit back in 2019, it wasn’t clear that the brand had a future. 

As many companies are wont to do, Google had good reason to ingest the accessory maker’s IP and set fire to the rest — but that didn’t happen. After a few fallow years, Fitbit became the software powering the Pixel Watch’s health capabilities, and is now shifting once again to working as a standalone hardware brand within Google.

	

After the monumental success of the Fitbit Air in May, the company is poised to release a Charge follow-up called the Edge. The Charge series hasn’t seen a refresh since 2023, and it appears that Google is updating its design and adding a number of app-like features that should bridge the proverbial gap between tracker and smartwatch.

Of course, Google may not have known Fitbit’s true trajectory back in 2019, but it’s arrived at a place that makes sense: Fitbit’s software is now tightly integrated into all of Google’s health-related endeavors, so the brand is pivoting back to hardware where it made its mark originally.

So the question is whether the Edge, or something like it, is the right move. The Air’s success came from its accessible price ($100) and the growing trend of screenless trackers. I wear a Fitbit Air alongside either a smartwatch or a regular one, and that’s its biggest appeal. And people are going to great lengths to hide the diminutive tracker in places most wearables can’t go. 

The Edge, on the other hand, is a traditional fitness tracker with a few tricks up its sleeve. Judging from the leaks, it will offer notifications, Google Maps, music controls, along with Find My Device support. And of course health tracking that, with a Google Health Premium account, includes an AI-powered fitness coach that’s proven its mettle over the past few months.

I doubt the Edge will have the same cultural impact as the Air, but I also see its existence as proof that Google understands why it bought Fitbit in the first place. Now that it’s plumbed the company for all of its wares, Fitbit rises once again where it all started: with cheap hardware that does just enough well to keep users happy.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Home Widget 1.10 is the fastest way to check every HomeKit camera at once
snippet: The Home app is a great place to configure your smart home, but it can be slow to control. The tab structure and room hierarchy make sense when you’re setting things up, but they add steps to everything you want to do fifty times a day. Home Widget builds the control panel that Apple didn’t. more…
fullText:
The Home app is a great place to configure your smart home, but it can be slow to control. The tab structure and room hierarchy make sense when you’re setting things up, but they add steps to everything you want to do fifty times a day. Home Widget builds the control panel that Apple didn’t.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Home Widget lets you build your own HomeKit control panels and place them on your home screen, lock screen, and more. Each panel is made up of tiles you configure yourself, with the icon, name, color, and size you choose, and each tile reflects the accessory’s current state meaning the lights are bright when they’re on and dim when they’re off. 

Your sensors will show their readings, and thermostats show the current temperature, all without opening the app. Panels sync across your devices through iCloud, and the app works entirely with what you’ve already set up in Apple’s Home app. It doesn’t replace anything; it just gives you a faster surface for your everyday tasks.

What’s new in 1.10

The camera mosaic is the major feature in 1.10. One tap on a Home Screen or Lock Screen widget, and every HomeKit camera appears in a single scrollable view. Tap any tile, and that camera fills the screen. You can also add a Control Center control that opens the mosaic or a specific camera directly. None of these actions involves launching the Home app.

Thermostat control and whole-room light actions are the two features that will matter most day-to-day for anyone with a larger HomeKit setup. You can now set your home temperature straight from a widget rather than opening the Home app or asking Siri. And rather than building a scene just to dim every light in a room, you can now toggle, dim, or change the color of an entire room from a single tile. Both of these closed real gaps between what a widget could do and what the native app could do.

1.10 also brings native iOS 26/27 widget appearances, including Clear, Tinted, Light, Dark, and Liquid Glass rendering, so panels adopt the wallpaper rather than sitting on top of it. Multi-sensor Matter accessories now show all their readings, and the app added richer Apple Watch integration.

With 1.10.2, thermostat support now extends to heating systems exposed as HeaterCooler, which covers a broader range of hardware. Search also now works when adding accessories, sensors, scenes, or other actions.

Wrap up

Home Widget is a free download, and you get up to three panels of up to seven tiles, with the icons and names of your choosing, and ten widget actions a day. The premium unlock ($14.99 one-time fee) removes those limits and opens the full set of settings. Monthly ($0.99) and yearly ($6.99) subscriptions are available as an alternative if you prefer to spread the cost.

If you have a lot of Apple Home accessories and you’re still doing most of your daily interactions inside the Home app, this is worth trying. Multiple cameras alone make the mosaic a good reason to install it.

You can download Home Widget for HomeKit from the App Store for free.

title: How to find out if Amazon thinks you have ‘flat buttocks’
snippet: "I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I’m literally speechless," one shopper wrote on Threads.
fullText:
It shouldn’t come as a surprise that Amazon collects data about you based on what you buy. If you buy a lot of cat litter, Amazon will probably infer that you have cats, or if you buy a lot of anti-acne skin products, then Amazon might guess you’re prone to breakouts. Even if we know that Amazon customizes our shopping experiences based on our purchase history, it still comes as a surprise to see all of these personal details laid out in a convenient list. Especially when those details get uncomfortably intimate.

One Threads user came across this section of her Amazon settings where you can see who the shopping giant thinks you are, and alongside more benign assumptions like “Shops from women’s departments” and “Probably owns a Shark robot vacuum,” she found that Amazon assumes she “has flat buttocks.”

“I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I’m literally speechless,” an Amazon customer, @fangirlinmegan, wrote on Threads. “I mean it ain’t wrong but damn did you have to call me out like that?”

In less than a day, the post garnered over a million views, including many from users who were curious what their own Amazon profiles might reveal. Here’s how you find out.

On desktop, you can find this page by hovering over where Amazon says “Hello, [your name]” in the upper right corner. Then click “Account” under the “Your Account” section. Under the “Ordering and shopping preferences” section, click “Your Shopping preferences.” From here, you can add in information of your own, like your shoe size, interests, and dietary preferences. But we’re not here to tell Amazon that it should stop selling you beef jerky since you’re a vegetarian. We’re here to see if Amazon thinks you have “flat buttocks.” When you scroll to the bottom of the page, you’ll see a blue hyperlinked option that says “Manage your information.” Once you click that, you’ll see what dirt Amazon has on you.

On the mobile app, you can get here by clicking the hamburger icon from the bottom menu bar, then navigating to Account > Shopping preferences > About you.

For me, Amazon has gleaned that I am someone who “practices photography,” “plays collectible card games,” and is “invested in the Apple ecosystem.” This is all true. Amazon has even flattered me by noting that I “read diverse non-fiction,” to which I say — why yes, I am indeed an open-minded intellectual with a thirst for knowledge. Thank you for noticing.

Other colleagues of mine found that Amazon correctly noted their interests in vinyl records and ceramics, as well as a penchant for “natural materials” in home decor and clothing that “prioritizes comfort.” None of us had anything as affronting as “has flat buttocks,” but the Threads user noted that this was likely because she had purchased “butt scrunch leggings.”

Tech companies know too much about us, and it’s jarring to realize just how closely they’re paying attention to how we use their platforms. We live in a world of alarming surveillance, but at least I know that Amazon doesn’t think my butt is flat.

snippet: Googlebooks don’t have the same level of web app support as Chromebooks, as only “compliant” apps can be installed, and that’s not the only regression from ChromeOS, as Linux apps don’t work in the same way either. more…
fullText:
Googlebooks don’t have the same level of web app support as Chromebooks, as only “compliant” apps can be installed, and that’s not the only regression from ChromeOS, as Linux apps don’t work in the same way either.

Googlebooks rely on Android apps and web apps for virtually all core functionality, with the Play Store actively directing users to which app is the most ideal on the platform. 

As it turns out, though, support for Progressive Web Apps on Googlebook isn’t quite at the same level as Chromebook. While most PWAs we’ve tried so far are easily installed, we ran into an issue installing the Slack PWA. Google, in a statement today, confirmed this is because Slack is not a “compliant” PWA, with Chromebooks instead relying on “manual installation.” It’s unclear what differs regarding Slack’s PWA — it functions just fine on other platforms such as Windows and ChromeOS — but it can’t be installed on Googlebook or Android devices.

Google says:

	

Installing PWAs is fully supported on Googlebooks. But, the Slack web app isn’t a compliant PWA. Chrome on ChromeOS allows manual installation even though it’s not a PWA. This capability will also be coming to Chrome on Googlebooks soon.

This mirrors another regression in app support compared to Chromebooks.

Googlebooks also, at least for now, lack the same level of Linux app support.

Chromebooks started adding support for installing Linux apps way back in 2018 and, after a few years in development, it became a secret super power of Google’s platform. Linux app support on Chromebook allowed users to bridge the app gap with the ability to install full desktop apps via Linux ports and, while it wasn’t the easiest process, it got the job done.

Googlebooks are in a very different state.

There’s little to no documentation around Linux apps on Googlebook right now, with Google’s only page on the matter describing how you can use the Terminal app to access a Debian command line interface. Google says:

You can use the Terminal app to access a powerful Debian Linux command-line environment directly on your Googlebook. You can install and run developer tools, code environments, and access other Linux applications. It expands your device’s capabilities for advanced tasks and software development.

But installing apps via this portal doesn’t put them within easy reach of the end user. It’s a far cry from Chromebook’s support, which placed most apps within the app drawer once they were installed. 

	

Google says that it’s possible to run apps, but that GUI apps “aren’t the main focus” of the Linux environment on Googlebook:

Just wanted to confirm that yes, there will be a Terminal app available on Googlebook out of the box, and yes it lets you run a Debian Linux environment on your device.

Also yes, you CAN run Linux GUI apps in this environment, but note that for this initial release of Googlebook, GUI apps aren’t the main focus. We’ll have more to share soon on the Terminal app!

One Linux user far more experienced than myself who dug into how Googlebook supports Linux apps, detailing that they show up in a single Terminal display window without their own Android windows or taskbar items. Another user saw the same behavior and noted reliability issues with GIMP, a popular photo editing app for Linux.

As mentioned, there’s no documentation yet on how to get Linux GUI apps running on Googlebook, so this is not functionality for the “average Joe” — not to say Linux apps on Chromebook were either, but it’s certainly odd to see that this has regressed in functionality rather than expanded.

title: iPhone Duo shows what the future of smartphones could look like
snippet: Since the unveiling of iPhone Duo, the idea of all major interface navigation elements being accessible from your thumb has been really interesting. Apple re-invented the idea of smartphone navigation with the outer display on iPhone Duo, and now it feels quite wrong that every smartphone puts things at the top. more…
fullText:
Since the unveiling of iPhone Duo, the idea of all major interface navigation elements being accessible from your thumb has been really interesting. Apple re-invented the idea of smartphone navigation with the outer display on iPhone Duo, and now it feels quite wrong that every smartphone puts things at the top.

Everyone yearns for the days of when phones were smaller, largely because things were more reachable. The downside to that is that, well, your screen is quite small, and the content landscape has evolved from that.

iPhone Duo solves both of these problems by still offering a reasonably large rectangular viewing area to the left of the dock and navigation area on the right. You still get a large viewing area, and you still have everything within a thumbs reach.

Ever since Apple showed this off, many enthusiasts have brought up the idea of an “iPhone Solo,” ie an iPhone Duo sized display, except it isn’t a foldable.

While I doubt Apple would offer this, I do think it’s quite an interesting idea, and maybe one day it could make sense depending on how well the iPhone Duo does. If you think about it, the current form factor of smartphones is a matter of happenstance. We had 16:9 displays, then we decided to axe all the bezels and the home button, which turned phones into this oddly tall device where things aren’t really reachable.

iPhone Duo rethought what a smartphone’s form factor should be. Apple didn’t merely slap normal iOS on the outside display and call it a day. They rethought it to make it optimal, and now I envy the fact that my phone is so tall.

	

We’ll see what happens. An iPhone Solo could easily happen if people receive the Duo’s outer screen well.

What do you think of the iPhone Solo concept? Would you buy one? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Call Screening has made a big difference to my iPhone experience
snippet: iOS 27 has brought a lot of new features to the iPhone, but one of the things that has made the biggest difference to my experience of the device as a phone actually dates back a year earlier. Apple introduced Call Screening to the Phone app in iOS 26, but I only started using it a few months ago – and the feature has protected me from a growing number of spam and spam calls … more…
fullText:
iOS 27 has brought a lot of new features to the iPhone, but one of the things that has made the biggest difference to my experience of the device as a phone actually dates back a year earlier.

Apple introduced Call Screening to the Phone app in iOS 26, but I only started using it a few months ago – and the feature has protected me from a growing number of spam and spam calls …

I’ve tried to be reasonably protective of my phone number, only providing it when it is not only demanded by an organization, but where I accept that it will be useful for them to have it. In many cases where a web form insists on it, I’ve used a fictitious number.

The UK’s telecoms regulator actually provides a range of 1,000 mobile numbers that have never been allocated so I can be sure my fake number won’t lead to someone else being spammed.

However, I’ve owned my mobile number for literally decades now, so it’s unavoidable that it has made its way onto some marketing lists, and there are also companies that use robocallers to dial random numbers. I haven’t been bothered by many of these historically, but for some reason there was a significant uptick earlier this year.

When Apple introduced the call screening feature last year, I was concerned about missing genuine calls, so didn’t immediately enable it. However, I did so earlier this year, selecting the Ask Reason for Calling option, and I have to say I highly recommend it.

The main spam/scam calls I received were from companies pretending to be my mobile carrier. I think some are likely third-party resellers hoping to trick me into switching network, while others are either trying to obtain payment details or carry out more general data harvesting. I’ve never let any of these calls get far enough to find out, but it reached the point where I was getting at least one of these calls every week. I’d also been getting a growing number of job scam calls.

Since switching on the feature, not a single one of these has got through to me. I think in the vast majority of cases, they immediately hang up when they get the automated response, while a few of them have bothered to give me their claimed reason for the call, and it’s been immediately obvious that I should reject it.

I also haven’t seen any indication of anyone genuine failing to reach me. I’ve had a number of genuine calls get filtered by the screening feature, but all of these have explained who they are and the reason for the call, and I’ve then been able to answer it.

If you don’t currently have Call Screening enabled, I highly recommend it. Open the Settings app, scroll down to the App section, select Phone, and then scroll down to Screen Unknown Callers.

title: Apple may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU in a tax compromise
snippet: Apple and other tech giants may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU under a modified version of a digital services tax plan. The EU hopes a revised version of earlier proposals will enable it to raise tax revenues without incurring the wrath of the White House … more…
fullText:
Apple and other tech giants may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU under a modified version of a digital services tax plan.

The EU hopes a revised version of earlier proposals will enable it to raise tax revenues without incurring the wrath of the White House …

There has long been debate within EU countries about taxes on digital services, with Apple examples including iCloud, Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Creator Studio, and more.

Some point to the significant revenues earned from selling subscription services to EU citizens without necessarily paying any tax in Europe on these receipts. Others are concerned that a digital tax could disproportionately hit European companies, while yet others are concerned about threatened retaliation by the White House for additional taxes on US companies.

The Financial Times reports that the European Commission has now come up with a compromise it hopes will keep everybody happy – other than the companies like Apple, Google and Meta who would be paying the new taxes, of course.

Brussels was considering changes to an existing proposal that would require all companies operating in the EU with revenue of more than €100mn a year to pay an annual lump-sum tax contribution, the officials said […] 

Adjusting the thresholds and contributions under the Core proposal to cover only very large corporates would both increase the amount raised from tech groups and defuse criticism in Europe that Core would hit many medium-sized European companies, officials argued.

The revised version of the plan would not single out companies selling digital services, but would apply to all large corporations. Since it was the former proposal that led the White House to threaten retaliatory tariffs, the EU hopes that the new version won’t provoke a new trade war with the US.

The amount that would be levied on each company has not yet been decided. The plan is to seek agreement on the principle across the 27 EU countries before setting a rate for the tax.

9to5Mac’s Take

This whole mess was supposed to have been resolved by a global agreement, brokered by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). This would have ensured that all companies worldwide pay at least some taxes in each of the countries in which they operate, and the plan had Apple’s support.

However, Donald Trump withdrew the US from this agreement, leading to calls for an EU-specific version. The idea that Trump won’t object to the revised plan seems to me rather optimistic.

title: Facer revamps Wear OS watch face library, adding new styles from Timex and more
snippet: Facer provides a huge library of watch faces for Wear OS and, with a new update, it’s adding even more styles while also redesigning the app entirely. more…
fullText:
Facer provides a huge library of watch faces for Wear OS and, with a new update, it’s adding even more styles while also redesigning the app entirely.

Available with the latest update, Facer now divides up its watch face library into a handful of categories. These include direct recommendations and categories such as entertainment, watch brands, and sports.

Facer explains:

For You: Your new personalized home where you will see watch faces from designers and styles you love.

Entertainment: Your space for officially licensed watch faces from your favorite brands like Fallout, PAC-Man, Star Trek, Tetris, and more!

Watch Brands: A new space dedicated to traditional watchmakers like MVMT, Maurice Lacroix, and Fortis, and the digital versions of their most popular watch models.

Facer Originals: a new program dedicated to supporting the most exceptional watch face designers worldwide, exclusively available on Facer. Learn more about Facer Originals

Health & Fitness: Find function-focused designs that put useful information at a glance, including steps, heart rate, and activity data, and more.

Sports: Explore collections around the sports you follow, from basketball and baseball to soccer and racing.

Facer is also introducing new watch faces in collaboration with Timex, Angry Birds, and Sonic the Hedgehog. Faces from Timex watches such as Marlin, Expedition, and T80 will all be available “this Fall” alongside existing faces from brands like MVMT, Maurice Lacroix, and Fortis.

	

A new “Facer Originals” program is also debuting to spotlight exclusive faces from designers on the platform.

title: Here’s everything new in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 [Gallery]
snippet: Google today rolled out Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 in quick succession to start a new preview cycle ahead of an expected March 2027 stable launch. more…
fullText:
Google today rolled out Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 in quick succession to start a new preview cycle ahead of an expected March 2027 stable launch.

	

Over the coming hours, we’ll dive into all of Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1’s new features and every single change. (The newest updates will be at the top of this list. Be sure to check back often and tell us what you find in the comments below.) Android 17 QPR2 Beta 6.1 screenshots appear on the left and Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 on the right.

If you want to quickly install Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 on your compatible Pixel 6a, Pixel 7, Pixel 7 Pro, Pixel 7a, Pixel Tablet, Pixel Fold, Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8a, Pixel 9, Pixel 9 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro XL, Pixel 9 Pro Fold, Pixel 9a, Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, Pixel 10 Pro Fold, Pixel 10a, Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold be sure to check out our step-by-step guide.

Updating…

New Notes QS Tile 

With the Android 17 QPR2 Beta, Google enabled the Notes lockscreen shortcut and homescreen widget/app shortcut for Pixel 11 devices.

As of QPR3 Beta 1, that’s still the case, with Notes not appearing on our Pixel 10.

This new beta adds a new Notes Quick Settings Tile for the Pixel 11 series.

Status bar tweaks

The changes made in the Android 17 QPR1 stable release are intentional after all.

There’s a bolder VPN icon, while the silent icon matches the volume menu.

Some icons, like Bluetooth and Airplane Mode, are slightly larger.

Gemini Intelligence boot screen on Pixel 10 series + more

On our Pixel 10, the Gemini Intelligence boot animation from the Pixel 11 series appears after installing QPR3 Beta 1.

Additionally, Proactive Assistance appears in system Settings. It’s now above Magic Cue, which remains available. Something similar happening during the QPR2 Beta but was later removed.

However, Proactive Assistance does not appear in Gemini app settings.

Fixes

Audio output device cannot be switched while playing audio from apps without active media controls. (Issue #259180936)

Apps crash when attempting to start a foreground service from a Quick Settings tile. (Issue #299506164)

Application icons in the app menu display with excessive spacing. (Issue #316288379, Issue #300758716)

App previews fail to display in the recent apps screen. (Issue #515091621)

NFC service crashes with DeadObjectException and stops detecting tags after the initial scan on Android 16. (Issue #456078994)

Device freezes and becomes unresponsive when unlocking with the fingerprint sensor. (Issue #490719716, Issue #514867650, Issue #523022829)

Device crashes when selecting the require eyes to be open option in Face Unlock settings. (Issue #466618368, Issue #522677686)

title: Pixel 11 Pro vs. iPhone 18 Pro: Copy-copy-paste or just copy-paste [Video]
snippet: There’s a new phone in town, and like the Pixel 11 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro looks eerily similar to what we saw last year. What can we glean from this duo? Here’s what you need to know. more…
fullText:
There’s a new phone in town, and like the Pixel 11 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro looks eerily similar to what we saw last year. What can we glean from this duo? Here’s what you need to know.

Same, same, and same again

If you wanted to critique the smartphone industry in Western markets, there are no two devices more obvious to use as the basis for your argument. There is something very familiar about the Pixel 11 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro – two phones that are almost the same as their predecessors.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Hardware progress has almost ground to a halt, which is both a fair criticism and maybe an admission that there really isn’t much left to do on those ubiquitous products we carry each and every day.

	

A smartphone is a tool. It’s your wallet, your mobile shopping card, your digital camera; it’s more than something you want, it’s an essential.

Maybe that is why we haven’t seen the two of the world’s biggest tech companies try to veer away from the “safe” designs they’ve peddled for a couple of years. It could be that we, the buyers of these products, similarly don’t care now.

Realistically, you could just read our deeper dive comparing the iPhone 17 Pro to the Pixel 11 Pro, and you’d get 95% of the way there. However, there are a few changes worth noting, given that Apple is still the top dog in the US market and dominates global sales in the “premium” segment. Google has been using Apple’s playbook, following a tried-and-tested path to some relative success as of late.

And so, we have two phones that look identical to the previous generation. Barely any visual cues save the colors to differentiate. It’s an indictment of where phones are today in some ways.

Camera goods and gimmicks

As far as I can tell, there are only two major changes to the iPhone 18 Pro. A smaller Dynamic Island and a variable aperture for the main lens. The camera aperture has been lauded somewhat, and it’s an interesting addition for a number of reasons.

Samsung experimented with the concept years ago when mobile sensors were significantly smaller, but the implementation here is different. Because modern smartphone sensors have such small pixels, you typically avoid ‘stopping down’ to prevent diffraction. 

However, since Apple widened the base aperture to f/1.4 to improve low-light intake by 50%, the variable aperture now serves as a necessary ‘stop’ to balance image sharpness and exposure control in brighter conditions. Ultimately, this provides more flexibility for videographers, though you’ll probably notice zero difference in daily photography.

The only changes to depth of field are when you get super close to a subject when shooting wide open. I found there were no visual changes to speak of. I’m not even sure it would help for videos, but I will give credit to Apple because the company is trying to give photographers and videographers more manual controls. Right now, it isn’t exactly doing much, but it could be something bigger, better, and more impressive with future updates – despite not really doing as much right now.

I still vastly prefer images from my own Pixel 11 Pro. It’s a vastly more flexible camera experience, bolstered tremendously with the addition of Camera Looks. Having those sensor-level controls makes for a very powerful piece of the Pixel camera system. Without going too deep into the video modes, yes, the iPhone 18 Pro feels like it’s catered to amateurs and professionals more readily than the Pixel 11 Pro.

HiLight is the only other differentiation, and it is, well, there if you care about soft LED lights on the back of your phone.

I talked about a bit of a gap, and you don’t need me to tell you that the A20 chip runs rings around the Tensor G6. Yes, it’s more powerful. It does more, it is more efficient, it’s not exactly a fair comparison.

Obviously, each chip is tuned to its respective OS, so it’s not really one-to-one, but yes, the iPhone 18 Pro is just more powerful without requiring cloud-based or AI functionality to plug some gaps. I think this is where the Pixel can flex some muscle.

Gemini and the functions it enables are more sensibly enabled because they’re passive. Not something you have to seek out. It’s one of the ways in which the Pixel and Proactive Assistance can feel futuristic, as it is doing everything with so little effort.

Apple teased something like this a few years ago, but there’s not enough there yet with Siri to meaningfully move the needle compared to what Google is doing with Gemini. That said, the two experiences outside of AI are just not all that different today. Android and iOS aren’t separated by much. Use apps, play games, send messages, take calls, browse the web. Which you prefer is ultimately up to what you prioritize.

Does the Pixel 11 Pro come up short against the iPhone 18 Pro?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

There isn’t much to really talk about on either device because there is so much similar to last year. If you wanted to save some money, the most sensible thing would be to look back a year. Get either the Pixel 10 Pro or the iPhone 17 Pro. Save your money, get a new case, replace the battery, just make do and mend.

We’re here to discuss the merits, though, and while the gap at times feels quite large, I do think that Google has been diligently working on the Pixel lineup to the stage that most people will be very happy with their purchase. I hoped more would change, but there feels like some artificial brakes have been pumped this time on the Pixel 11 Pro. The iPhone 18 Pro is playing backup to the Duo this year, so it was always less of a priority for the company, even if it will be the biggest seller. 

Google doesn’t really have that excuse to lean on. All of the Pixel 11 phones are basically identical to the previous gen.

Then again, if we are being 100% honest with ourselves, does Apple deserve more criticism than Google for not moving the needle, given that the current crop of Pixel devices lacks a little more in certain key areas? It’s really frustrating to admit that, yes, there are more compromises on a Pixel 11 Pro than an iPhone 18 Pro across almost every area. The Pixel edges the iPhone in AI functionality and maybe stills photography, but the scoresheet isn’t exactly flattering.

To be blunt, this is not glazing the iPhone. It’s important to be objective, and objectively, you just get more for your money with the iPhone this year (again). No, I won’t be switching any time soon, and I likely won’t even keep hold of an iOS device this year, but in some ways, Apple deserves some plaudits as even without much change, the overall package still surpasses a similarly priced and similarly unchanged Pixel 11 Pro.

title: You can unlock a Googlebook’s bootloader, Magisk support in the works
snippet: Googlebook is an Android-based platform and, with that, comes the potential to do a bit more with it. Google has confirmed you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook, and now Magisk root support is already in the works. more…
fullText:
Googlebook is an Android-based platform and, with that, comes the potential to do a bit more with it. Google has confirmed you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook, and now Magisk root support is already in the works.

On a support page, Google details how you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook. Google says that a “developer or advanced user can unlock their device’s bootloader to install a custom version of the operating system or test an app,” but stresses that “most users don’t need to unlock their Googlebook’s bootloader.”

Like on a Pixel or other Android phone that easily supports bootloader unlock, you’ll need to enable OEM unlocking via the Settings menu and Developer options, then press and hold Esc + F2 and press the power button, releasing all keys when the screen lights up. From there, bootloader unlock is located under “advanced options.”

And, with that, root support is also coming.

	

Magisk developer John Wu confirmed on Twitter/X that support for Magisk is in the works for Googlebook. In a separate post, Wu called Googlebook “the ideal platform for Android modding” since modern Android smartphones suffer from broken apps including banking apps when they are rooted. Wu says that there are some tweaks needed to bring Magisk and, in turn, all of the benefits that come with a rooted device to Googlebook, but it’s coming.

snippet: Following last month’s addition of Gemini control, Google is rolling out a sizable Pixel Buds Pro, Pro 2, and Pixel Buds 2a firmware update. more…
fullText:
Following last month’s addition of Gemini control, Google is rolling out a sizable Pixel Buds Pro, Pro 2, and Pixel Buds 2a firmware update.

The only feature exclusive to the Pixel Buds Pro 2 is Dynamic Active Noise Cancellation. Google will “automatically adjust audio or noise cancellation based on your ear seal.” This compensates for “subtle shifts” when the buds move in your ear.

The remaining features are available for the Pixel Buds Pro (2022), Pro 2 (2024), and 2a (2025). When these features were previewed in August, Google did not mention that the original Pro model would be getting this update.

With last month’s Pixel Buds companion app update, you can turn on Active Noise Cancellation, adjust EQ, and enable touch controls with Gemini voice commands.

	
	

During phone calls, Tap to Mute lets you mute and unmute the microphone by tapping the buds. This gesture requires a paired Pixel phone.

Pixel Buds can now auto-pause media playback when you fall asleep, which is determined by Pixel Watch sleep sensing. This will also disable touch gestures and silence notifications.

The final update is Enhanced Live Translate that allows you to “leave your phone in your pocket and start translating instantly with a simple touch on your earbuds.”

Whether you’re conversing with someone or using listening mode to stay aware of your surroundings in a foreign language, Pixel Buds work seamlessly with the Google Translate app to make on-the-go translation easier than ever.

Make sure you’re running the latest version of the Pixel Buds app, and be on the lookout for software release_6.144. Open the companion client and scroll down for More settings > Firmware update to check.

title: Apple confirms iPhone 18 Pro Max AT&T cellular issues, affected devices require hardware replacement
snippet: Apple has confirmed an issue causing a “small number” of iPhone 18 Pro Max devices on AT&T to lose cellular service. Apple released software and carrier updates to prevent the issue from affecting additional users, but the company tells 9to5Mac that devices that have already lost service will require a hardware replacement. more…
fullText:
Apple has confirmed an issue causing a “small number” of iPhone 18 Pro Max devices on AT&T to lose cellular service. 

Apple released software and carrier updates to prevent the issue from affecting additional users, but the company tells 9to5Mac that devices that have already lost service will require a hardware replacement.

In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

“We have identified an issue affecting a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network that may cause a device to lose service and be unable to make calls. We released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week and strongly encourage all iPhone 18 Pro Max users to update now, and are also issuing a carrier settings update today. These updates together are meant to help prevent this issue from occurring.”

The carrier settings update for the iPhone 18 Pro Max will download automatically over the next 14 days. However, users can manually trigger the download by going to Settings, choosing General, then About.

Apple explains that the software updates will help prevent future issues for iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T. The software updates will not restore service on devices that have already lost it.

Apple says that iPhone 18 Pro Max users who have already lost service will need a hardware replacement. Those users should contact Apple Support or AT&T, or visit an Apple Store or AT&T location. 

As we reported this morning, iPhone 18 Pro Max users affected by this problem can’t connect to AT&T’s network for calls, texts, and data. Instead, those users see “SOS” in their iPhone’s status bar. The connectivity issues aren’t impacting every iPhone 18 Pro Max user on AT&T. 

Interestingly, the iPhone 18 Pro Max in the United States uses a Qualcomm modem. The iPhone 18 Pro, which uses Apple’s C2 modem, is unaffected by these AT&T connectivity issues.
