title: Google Pixel 2 XL set the stage for a decade of ups and downs
snippet: Google Pixel’s 10-year anniversary has me taking a look back at a bunch of the milestones throughout this lineup’s history and, when picking up the Pixel 2 XL, hindsight really kicked in as to how this phone was very much a sign of the tumultuous roller coaster that would become Google Pixel. more…
fullText:
Google Pixel’s 10-year anniversary has me taking a look back at a bunch of the milestones throughout this lineup’s history and, when picking up the Pixel 2 XL, hindsight really kicked in as to how this phone was very much a sign of the tumultuous roller coaster that would become Google Pixel.

The original Google Pixel hit the ground running and really did a great job pitching itself. A stellar camera was the main selling point, but Google’s thoughtful software, well-designed hardware, and ecosystem as a whole filled in the bigger picture to deliver a product that, outside of minor gripes, was about as “perfect” as you could ask for from an initial debut in a product category.

Fast-forward to a year later and, oof.

The Pixel 2 and Pixel 2 XL both arrived with some welcome upgrades across the board, but it was also abundantly clear that Google made some serious missteps. The smaller Pixel 2 was a tame revision in basically every way and, outside of the mega-thick bezels, was still a perfectly fine phone.

	

Pixel 2 XL, though, had some glaring flaws.

While I can look back fondly now on many aspects of the Pixel 2 XL, it’s wild in hindsight that a company at Google’s scale, even nearly a decade ago, made such a massive blunder. The Pixel 2 XL’s overall hardware stuck the landing. The updated dual-tone design still has that iconic “Panda” look and the colorful accent button that lived on through prior generations, but the glaring flaw on this device was the display. 

The LG-made panel was horribly inconsistent. In the best-case scenario, you’d get a panel with not-great viewing angles, slightly off colors, and burn-in issues. Worst case, a panel with a blue tint, black smears, and/or a grainy look. I still remember feeling like it was playing the lottery with buying this device and exchanging it to get a “good” one. Google tweaked this over time with software as well as by upping the warranty coverage, but it was still a huge problem with an otherwise great design.

And, in hindsight, that was kind of a signal of what was to come for Pixel as a whole.

	

The Pixel 2 XL tried something new and ultimately fell short, leading to a big correction the following year. Pixel 3 had a stunning display by comparison, and even to this day, Google has invested heavily in giving its phones some of the best displays you can find. The same pattern has been found throughout the lineup. New swings lead to new problems, with Google ultimately scrambling to make the best of it through software updates and making corrections later on. A similarly big problem came with 2020’s Pixel 6 series, with the modem in the first Tensor chip being truly terrible, but Google working to make the best of it in later software updates, only to iterate on the modem with each new generation to the point where, today, Tensor’s modem is roughly on par with anyone else in the ways that matter most.

Google Pixel remains a series that delivers ups and downs through each new generation, but it’s also clearer that the company has finally settled into something that works in 2026. Where the Pixel 2 XL was still in an era where Google would pivot on a whim, the Pixel 11 series comes from a place of stability, predictability, and at least mild success.

Microsoft’s keynote will start at 10AM PT / 1PM ET on Wednesday October 7th. The full presentation should run for around an hour. You can watch it live on YouTube, but the best way to follow along is through our live blog.

What to expect from Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event

Surface Laptop Ultra. Microsoft already unveiled its MacBook Pro competitor earlier this year, but we’re still waiting on pricing, release dates, and full specs. I’d expect we’ll get all of these details and lots more. Rumors suggest Microsoft will release multi configurations of the Laptop Ultra, with 18-core and 20-core CPU variants and RAM configurations all the way up to 128GB.

RTX Spark platform. Jensen Huang will appear on stage, so we’re likely to get even more details on Nvidia’s effort to shake-up the Windows laptop market. Microsoft might have the hero device, but there are plenty of OEMs also preparing to launch RTX Spark-powered laptops.

Windows AI agent news. I expect we’ll hear a lot more about Microsoft’s plans to have AI agents running locally on Windows. The Surface Laptop Ultra supercharges these kind of agents thanks to Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips, and Microsoft has already been laying the groundwork for AI agents in Windows for nearly a year now.

title: Ring’s Debut Smart Lock Solves the Category’s Biggest Issue: Dead Battery Lockouts
snippet: Ring’s foray into smart locks brings a first-of-its-kind feature that solves one of the categories biggest pain points.
fullText:
Smart locks are becoming the norm, not the exception, for homeowners who value security. They’re mostly straightforward, affordable and user-friendly, but because smart locks are rarely hardwired, they rely on standard replaceable or rechargeable batteries. Therein lies the biggest smart lock pain point: keeping the battery charged so you don’t inadvertently lock yourself out.

Until now, most smart locks have relied on an old-fashioned key as a backup if the lock dies, along with some experiments with solar panels. Ring’s first entry into the smart lock category, announced today and dubbed The Ring Smart Lock, uses a supercapacitor, a first-of-its-kind energy crank built into the thumbturn. 

Ring has finally entered the smart lock chat with a hand-rechargeable unit.David Watsky/CNET

The small knob fixed below the backlit touchscreen keypad charges the smart lock with just a few turns, giving it roughly 20 seconds of operation – enough time to get in the house and, hopefully, throw your battery on the charger. We got a first look at the lock during a private demonstration by Ring Founder, CEO and brains behind the debut smart lock, Jamie Siminoff.

			

More from CNET

A small display screen (not included with the lock) showed how quickly the lock could be temporarily charged—roughly four or five spins. The crank operates no matter how dead the battery is. In fact, it’ll work even with the battery completely removed, Siminoff said. 

Ring’s energy crank charges the smart lock just long enough to get inside. David Watsky/CNET

When developing the lock, Siminoff couldn’t believe most were still relying on keys as backup, a tool he refers to as “medieval” in its simplicity and fallibility. Other emergency backup entry systems, including portable power banks with USB-C ports hidden in the lock or 9-volt battery chargers, present their own complications and duly require the user to carry a physical piece of equipment or hide it somewhere accessible. 

Most smart locks include a traditional physical keyhole for emergencies.

John Carlsen/CNET

Supercapacitors store electrical energy electrostatically rather than through chemical reactions. They store energy quickly, in this case through the physical cranking, but for only a short period. As Siminoff explained, a smart lock is the perfect use case for this short-burst energy-storage technology. 

	

			

	

			

									

						The Best Smart Locks, Tested by CNET					

							

		

Ring’s crowning innovation is the energy crank, but the sleek smart lock also includes many industry-standard features, including remote locking and unlocking via app, an onboard fingerprint reader, and integration with the Ring and Amazon device ecosystem, including Alexa. 

Beyond the energy crank, Ring’s $249 model includes many standard smart lock features, including a fingerprint reader and remote app control.

The Ring Smart Lock stays connected through Amazon Sidewalk, a shared network powered by Amazon devices in the area. That means it doesn’t need Wi-Fi for remote locking and status updates.

Ring will sell the Smart Lock for $249 starting in 2027.

title: ‘HomePad’ coming: Will Apple hold an October special event?
snippet: With Apple reportedly planning to unveil new products on October 13, here’s when the company could announce an event, based on the timing of its previous October announcements. more…
fullText:
With Apple reportedly planning to unveil new products on October 13, here’s when the company could announce an event, based on the timing of its previous October announcements.

Will Apple hold an October event?

While Apple’s September event history tends to follow a very predictable pattern, the company’s October event history is much less precise, both in terms of when the events are held and how far in advance they are announced.

Since 2010, Apple has held an October event just 10 times, with the most recent one being the Halloween-themed “Scary Fast” event on the evening of October 30, 2023.

Here’s how far in advance Apple has announced each of its October events since 2010:

That said, Bloomberg recently reported that Apple plans to unveil its long-rumored smart home hub, a new generation of the HomePod mini, and a new Siri AI-powered Apple TV 4K on Tuesday, October 13, though it did not specify whether the company will hold an event to announce the products.

If that turns out to be the case, Apple could potentially announce the event as early as next Monday, October 5, but likely no later than Wednesday, October 7.

It’s worth noting that Apple is also expected to announce an OLED iPad mini, new iMacs, and several new MacBook Pros, including touchscreen models, in 2026. So it remains to be seen whether some of those products would be unveiled at the same event, at a separate event, or through press releases.

Looking back, Apple announced new Macs through press releases over three consecutive days in October 2024, while in October 2025, it unveiled the M5 chip alongside new iPad Pro, MacBook Pro, and Apple Vision Pro models without holding an event.

By contrast, Apple has only held a November event once, in 2020, when its “One More Thing” event introduced the first Macs powered by the M1 Apple silicon chip.

Of course, 2020 was an unusual year for Apple’s event schedule, with the company also holding separate events in September and October after a rare late-June WWDC, as the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted its usual timeline.

fullText:

title: 15 years after his passing, nobody is ‘The Next Steve Jobs’
snippet: Today marks 15 years since Steve Jobs passed away after a long battle with pancreatic cancer. Every year, memories come flooding back, and this one is no different. When I was contemplating what I wanted to say about Steve today, it occurred to me that much of what I or anyone has ever wanted to say about him has already been said. more…
fullText:
Today marks 15 years since Steve Jobs passed away after a long battle with pancreatic cancer. Every year, memories come flooding back, and this one is no different. When I was contemplating what I wanted to say about Steve today, it occurred to me that much of what I or anyone has ever wanted to say about him has already been said.

He changed my life, and he rewrote the fabric of society. But there’s one part of his legacy that’s worth reflecting on: he introduced hundreds of millions of people to the simple idea of making something great for others.

Of course, he did it on a much grander scale than many of us ever will. He saw it as ‘expressing appreciation for the species.’ We often talk about his belief that we should strive to put a “dent in the universe,” but we don’t talk enough about how there are many ways to do that, at varying levels, and with different motivations. It can mean so many different things to so many people. 

As I’ve been reading through Ron Johnson’s new book “Shop Different,” I’ve been transported back through some vivid storytelling to when Ron and Steve were gearing up to debut the first Apple Stores. The book paints a detailed, arguably beautiful picture of Steve; complicated as ever, but meticulous and thoughtful. 

He’s often remembered for how hard he pushed people to do their best work, but what’s crystal clear is how much he loved learning from those same people.

Ron Johnson says he proposed the idea of ‘loving your customers’ when they were planning Apple’s retail philosophy. Steve was uncomfortable with the word “love” in that context, but years later, from the Town Hall stage during the iPhone 4 ‘antennagate’ press conference, he laid it out on a simple slide that said, “We love our users.” Looking back, it feels as though the love and care were there all along, even if Steve didn’t realize it. His curiosity and care for the people who would use his products feel increasingly rare today. Apple’s original phrase, ‘enrich lives,’ expressed the same aspiration in more secular terms. Making something easier or simpler isn’t the same as enriching a life.

	

Ever since he passed away, it’s been a common refrain to call someone ‘the next Steve Jobs’. I always look to those who knew him the best. They had the clearest view of his motivations. No one else in the industry comes close to earning the mantle of ‘the next Steve Jobs’ because no one can check every box. I’m not sure today’s tech culture could foster someone with that same extraordinary combination of traits. You can be a visionary, you can make incredible products, you can put a ‘dent in the universe,’ but there was more to Steve than just that. 

Looking for ‘the next Steve Jobs’ misses what made him so special. He cared about every detail more than anybody else, learned humility, took responsibility, and focused on unlocking creativity rather than how many eyeballs he could claim or keystrokes he could collect. Steve simply wanted to make the best products to help people unlock their creativity. His high standards were certainly a part of his success, but so was his heart. The more we learn about Steve, the clearer that becomes.

Maybe the point shouldn’t be to find ‘the next Steve Jobs,’ but to remember what he showed us: that technology can be ambitious and earthshaking while still being deeply human. The best products are driven by love for the people who will use them, as much as by business metrics.

There are many ways to put a ‘dent in the universe,’ but I believe Steve was referring to one: making wonderful tools that could help anyone create something of their own and feel the care that went into making those tools. More of us should strive to model his mission.

title: A Surface Laptop Ultra? What to Expect for Microsoft’s Oct. 7 Event
snippet: The much-rumored Surface Laptop Ultra, with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip, could get a release date.
fullText:
After a summer full of folding iPhones and Googlebooks, Microsoft is getting ready for a new laptop-centered event this week. The company is hosting a Windows and Surface event on Wednesday in San Francisco, its first laptop event in two years. This is everything we’re expecting to see — and no, sorry, Windows 12 is not on the list.

The event will be a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC,” according to Microsoft. That makes sense as Microsoft has been all-in on AI by incorporating Copilot everywhere and partnering with chip makers like Qualcomm to bring enough firepower to its devices to handle the computational load of generative and agentic AI tasks. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and the head of Windows and Devices, Pavan Davuluri, are slated to speak.

This event could be when Microsoft actually drops the Surface Laptop Ultra, a 15-inch high-end variant first announced this spring at Computex. The Ultra is powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip, so Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s slated appearance at the event is another sign toward the Ultra. 

			

More from CNET

We already got two new Surface laptops this month, previewed at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit. At the Hawaii event, Microsoft upgraded its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface 13-inch laptops, running on Snapdragon Elite X2 chips, and introduced a new Surface mouse to go along with them. The new laptops have better cameras and “embody the PC-phone marriage Qualcomm promised years ago,” CNET’s David Lumb reports.

A big question will be prices. Computer hardware companies have raised their prices across the board, from Apple to Asus and Acer, over the last year to keep up with rising manufacturing costs. AI is at least partially to blame, with advanced chips in hot demand for data centers as well as laptops and phones. Other costs, like price increases in Windows licenses during the manufacturing process, may also be contributing to higher price tags. The result, sometimes called RAMageddon, is that it’s more expensive to buy new devices.

How to watch Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event

The keynote begins at 10 a.m. PT / 1 p.m. ET on Wednesday, Oct. 7., and it’s expected to last about one hour. The event is being held in San Francisco and will be livestreamed on Window’s YouTube channel. CNET will be on the ground to bring you all the latest Microsoft news.

Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens.
